source.title: Visualizing high-dimensional loss landscapes with Hessian directions

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies loss-landscape projections and reports training and test performance around trained solutions. It discusses generalization, but does not test the claim versions' specified interventions or measure their specified training–test gap relationships.
record.gate_note: The paper's discussion of flatness and generalization does not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness-to-gap relationship in V7. Its reported projection results concern changes in loss and accuracy near trained solutions; they do not test V1–V8 as specified.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether random loss projections preserve curvature and compares performance at projection minima. It does not test V1–V8. Its argument against interpreting random-projection flatness as generalization evidence does not evaluate V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking of generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors show that random projections can conceal saddles and produce apparent flatness through cancellation of opposite curvatures, caution against using such flatness as a generalization measure, and propose dominant Hessian projections. They regard optimization benefits as promising but requiring further research.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes local loss geometry using random and dominant Hessian directions; it does not use the memorization, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, regularization, sharpness-gap, or example-removal recipes in the versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Projection direction changes the depicted loss geometry and reported local minima. In the function-approximation examples, the training and test loss minima differ between random and Hessian projections.

fits_no_version.finding: Random projections can conceal saddle geometry; averaging positive and negative curvature can produce apparent flatness. Filter normalization in the classifier experiments does not establish a sharpness–generalization-gap correlation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent flatness in random low-dimensional loss projections can misrepresent the curvature of the original loss landscape.

fits_no_version.finding: Performance at training-loss minima in random and dominant-Hessian projection planes varies by architecture. DenseNet-121's Hessian minimum substantially lowers training loss while increasing test loss; the function approximators show reductions in both.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Moving to a lower training-loss point along dominant Hessian directions can improve or worsen held-out performance depending on the model and task.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment
record.problems: Projection minima are local results in selected two-dimensional domains; the paper notes that loss and accuracy are not proportional and that interpretation of performance variations is difficult. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported performance comparisons.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out performance under the same architecture and training recipe.
Test-error trends as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under specified tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce those effects.
Dropout interventions, training-set size, underfitting, and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus generalization gaps across comparably trained networks, including ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All seven rows compare the study's projection methods and should remain outside version-specific evidence. The geometric argument concerns random-projection flatness, not V7's specified magnitude-aware sharpness measure; it therefore warrants no V7 verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test-error trend.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons for image generalization.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes.
Dropout effects and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance compared with the training–test gap across networks.
Removing memorized examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

rows.note: These local projection comparisons do not measure the claim versions' training–test generalization-gap relationships.
